articles.title_orig: War of words over Xinjiang erupts between Chinese and Turkish social media users
articles.title_zh: War of words over Xinjiang erupts between Chinese and Turkish social media users
articles.content_orig:
The row comes amid a growing drive by Ankara to promote a pan-Turkic agenda that has proved to be sensitive area in relations with Beijing
The debate over ethnic identity in Xinjiang has triggered an online clash between Chinese and Turkish social media users.
The row began earlier this month when a Turkish social media user recalled an encounter with a Uygur from Xinjiang, the region in China that is home to nearly 12 million mainly Muslim Turkic speakers.
The user wrote that the woman did not look Chinese, but when asked whether she considered herself Turkic, the woman responded: “No, I’m Chinese.” The user also called on her to “return to your roots”.
The post had gained over 2 million views by Friday afternoon before the account was apparently deleted.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine must 'unblock' Patriot missile delivery, Zelenskyy says after deadly strikes - ABC News
articles.title_zh: Ukraine must 'unblock' Patriot missile delivery, Zelenskyy says after deadly strikes - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
At least four people were killed in Ukraine on Saturday evening.
LONDON -- Russian drone and missile attacks on multiple Ukrainian regions killed at least four people on Saturday night, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a post to social media on Sunday.
Ukraine's air force said Russia launched 153 drones along with an unspecified number of cruise missiles into the country in its latest round of attacks. The air force said that 119 drones were shot down or otherwise suppressed, with impacts reported in 15 locations.
Four people were killed by a Russian attack in the southeastern Dnipropetrovsk region on Saturday evening, Zelenskyy said, with another 22 people injured.
Zelenskyy said it was "crucial" to bolster Ukrainian defenses alongside renewed U.S.-led peace negotiations. "We need to unblock the already agreed-upon deliveries of interceptors for Patriot systems," the Ukrainian leader wrote, referring to the U.S.-made air defense system that has been key to Ukrainian efforts to blunt Russian ballistic missile attacks.
The tightening supply of Patriot batteries and their interceptor missiles has become a fraught diplomatic issue. The problem has been exacerbated by the ongoing U.S.-Israeli conflict with Iran, which has seen American and allied forces across the Middle East expend large numbers of interceptors to defend against Iranian ballistic missile and drone attacks.
Zelenskyy has repeatedly criticized the U.S. for failing to ensure an adequate supply of missiles. The Ukrainian leader told ABC News during an interview in Kyiv last week that his country needs to be supplied with around 350 Patriot interceptors each month to defend against Moscow's attacks.
Over the last three months, Zelenskyy said, Kyiv had received only 24 interceptor missiles.
Ukraine's State Emergency Service reported Russian strikes in the Dnipropetrovsk, Kharkiv, Zhytomyr and Vinnytsia regions on Saturday night into Sunday morning. At least six people were injured in the attack on Vinnytsia, the SES said, with four people -- among them three emergency workers -- also injured in the attack in Kharkiv.
Among the targets of the overnight Russian strikes were residential buildings, a hypermarket, thermal power plants, substations, coal mines and grain storage facilities, Zelenskyy said in a post to Telegram, adding that damage was reported in nine regions of Ukraine.
"This is how Russia reacts to diplomacy and efforts to isolate it," Zelenskyy said.
Russia's Defense Ministry, meanwhile, reported the interception of at least 532 Ukrainian drones overnight, with craft shot down over 22 Russian regions -- including Moscow -- plus occupied Crimea and the Black Sea.
Last week saw President Donald Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff travel to meet with Zelenskyy in the Norwegian capital of Oslo, followed by a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg.
Witkoff described the talks as "constructive," but deadly strikes continued in the days after his meetings with the Ukrainian and Russian leaders.
Fresh trilateral U.S.-Ukraine-Russia talks are expected to be held in the United Arab Emirates in November. In an interview with Kremlin propagandist Pavel Zarubin published on Sunday, Russian presidential aide Yuri Ushakov said that a possible deal between Moscow and Kyiv "still needs work."
Discussing the planned trilateral meeting in November, Ushakov said, "Not much could be decided during the first meeting too, it will perhaps be observational."

articles.title_orig: Brazil votes in tight runoff between leftist Lula and Bolsonaro Jr.
articles.title_zh: Brazil votes in tight runoff between leftist Lula and Bolsonaro Jr.
articles.content_orig:
Incumbent president lost in first round to senator and son of convicted ex-president
Brazilians are going to the polls on Sunday in a highly unpredictable runoff in which the leftist president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva , is attempting an unprecedented comeback against the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro , who won the first-round vote.
Bolsonaro’s surprise victory despite not leading most polls made him the favourite three weeks ago, but since then Lula’s campaign has gained ground, and the two go into the contest virtually tied.
The gap between them was the narrowest ever recorded in a first round, at less than 2% of the vote, and the 81-year-old president has spent much of the runoff campaign focused on turnout – abstention reached a record high in the first round and disproportionately affects his voters – and on stoking fears over what a return to power by a member of the Bolsonaro family could mean.
A congressman for more than 20 years with few bills passed, the 45-year-old Bolsonaro is the eldest son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro , who is under house arrest serving a 27-year sentence for attempting a coup to overturn his 2022 defeat to Lula.
The senator has promised that if elected he will pardon his father, and with an even more conservative congress taking office next year he has vowed to “change the constitution and re-democratise this country”, sending chills through those who fear he could follow in his father’s authoritarian footsteps.
“We’re facing two completely different projects for the country,” said voter Nuno Rau, 63, an architect and writer. “One points towards the end of social rights and the end of democracy itself; on the other side is someone who fought for income distribution and free public education. I may have criticisms of Lula, but there is no way to choose Bolsonaro,” he added.
Aparecida Moreira, a 62-year-old lawyer, will vote for Bolsonaro mainly because of the “iron fist” security policy he proposes, including building five “mega-prisons” inspired by those of El Salvador’s populist autocrat Nayib Bukele.
“I agree with Bolsonaro’s idea of chemical castration for rapists, because there is no crime worse than rape,” said Moreira, adding that voting for Lula would be the same as voting for the “dictator” Alexandre de Moraes , the justice who, despite not having been appointed by Lula, is widely associated with him by Bolsonaro supporters because he oversaw the former president’s conviction.
Both Flávio Bolsonaro and Lula drew large crowds to their final campaign rallies on Saturday in Rio de Janeiro, São Paulo and Belo Horizonte.
With each side of supporters virtually “crystallised”, the election will be decided by the small number of voters who identify with neither candidate.
Bolsonaro began the runoff campaign with a lead and the support of most other defeated candidates, but instead of growing, he stagnated in the polls while Lula gained support.
Many analysts saw this as the result of part of the population suddenly waking up to the “fear” of a Bolsonaro returning to power, as well as controversies including the fact that the senator is under investigation in two federal police inquiries over alleged corruption and money laundering.
Lula, by contrast, radically changed his digital strategy and benefited from student-led protests across the country, most of which did not even involve the president.
“In the first round, Lula’s campaign failed to connect with the population, but now it has been civil society movements that have driven his growth,” said the political scientist Helcimara de Souza Telles.
Whatever the result, the race is expected to be decided by a narrow margin in Latin America’s largest country, with an electorate of 159 million.
Many analysts believe that if Lula overturns his first-round defeat, Bolsonaro could follow his father’s example from four years ago and refuse to concede, and that Donald Trump, a longstanding ally of the Bolsonaro clan, could refuse to recognise the result.
“Trump wants to ‘colonise’ all of Latin America in pursuit of its own interests,” said Telles, adding that, with rightwing candidates having won all seven presidential elections held in Latin America since Trump began his second term, Brazil is one of the few countries in the region still offering any resistance to the US president.
“So a Bolsonaro victory would mean losing Brazil to a model of autocracy backed by the US,” she added.

articles.title_orig: Xinhua Headlines: Retracing an odyssey: Why people walk China's Long March 90 years later
articles.title_zh: Xinhua Headlines: Retracing an odyssey: Why people walk China's Long March 90 years later
articles.content_orig:
* This year marks the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Long March.
* People from China and abroad continue to retrace the Long March, some covering the entire route and others exploring sections by car or on foot.
* For many, the journey offers a way to learn about the Red Army's history, understand the CPC and see how China has changed over the decades.
BEIJING, Oct. 25 (Xinhua) -- One man, one horse and more than a year on the road.
In 2017, Luo Jianhua set out on horseback from Ruijin in east China to retrace the historic Long March. His wife, Ding Qimei, followed in a support vehicle.
Together, they crossed 81 counties and districts across 11 provincial-level regions before reaching Wuqi in northwest China, completing the journey in one year and nine days.
In 2024, Luo and Ding took to the road again with their daughter and grandniece, this time tracing the route of the Red Army's West Route Army.
Born into a farming family in southwest China's Guizhou Province, Luo grew up hearing stories of the Red Army from his elders. One saying stayed with him: "When life gets tough, think of the Red Army's 12,500-kilometer Long March."
Luo left school at 17 to make a living, later running businesses ranging from a coal-washing plant and a pig farm to an organic rice cultivation company.
While the stories he had heard as a child sustained him through difficult times, Luo long harbored a desire to experience firsthand what the Red Army had endured.
Hailed by American journalist Edgar Snow as "an odyssey unequaled in modern times," the Long March took place at a time when China was beset by foreign aggression, social turmoil and destitution.
Facing encirclement by overwhelming and much better-armed Kuomintang forces, the Communist Party of China (CPC)-led Red Army embarked on the epic military trek from 1934 to 1936.
During the march, the troops crossed nearly 100 rivers, traversed vast grasslands once known as a "death trap," and climbed over more than 40 mountains, including more than 20 snow-capped mountains rising above 4,000 meters.
This military maneuver gave the CPC a new foothold in northwest China, from which it built up its strength, fought back against invading Japanese troops and eventually toppled the corrupt Kuomintang regime, leading to the founding of the People's Republic of China in 1949.
For Luo, retracing the route made the Red Army's hardships that he had read about far more tangible.
In northwest Sichuan Province, he and his horse once sank into a marsh. As he struggled to free the animal, he thought about the soldiers who had crossed similar terrain decades earlier.
"I felt for them. They had so little food and equipment, yet they had to keep going through wind and hail. Some fell and never got up again," he said.
Luo is not alone. People from China and abroad continue to retrace the Long March, some covering the entire route and others exploring sections by car or on foot. For many, the journey offers a way to learn about the Red Army's history, understand the CPC and see how China has changed over the decades.
The Long March's reach has extended beyond China. First published in Britain in 1937, Snow's "Red Star Over China" introduced the Chinese revolution to international readers. Decades later, Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist Harrison Salisbury retraced the route and described the Long March as "a great human epic."
That appeal continues today. Dutch sinologist Elsbeth van Paridon, who joined a group retracing the route this summer, said walking the route gave her a feeling similar to looking out over the beaches of Normandy and realizing what had happened there.
She noted that the former revolutionary sites along the route now also serve as ecological parks, becoming part of a broader tourism economy that supports local development.
"That is how you see the spirit of the Long March live on," she said.
William N. Brown, a U.S. professor at Xiamen University who has lived in China for nearly 40 years, has retraced part of the route and witnessed the country's transformation firsthand.
He first traveled to Guizhou in 1994, when unpaved roads and limited river crossings left mountain communities isolated. Pointing to a towering bridge spanning a valley in Qinggangpo Village, Brown highlighted the region's staggering leap in connectivity.
"The most important change is invisible: people have gained confidence and self-respect," he said. "Thirty years ago, many thought prosperity would take 50 years to achieve -- they never expected to see it in their own lifetime."
THE SAME ROAD, A TRANSFORMED CHINA
The changes are also visible in the country's infrastructure. Roads now cut through mountains that Red Army soldiers once crossed on foot, while bridges span valleys and rivers that once posed major obstacles.
China's operational high-speed rail network has surpassed 50,000 kilometers, accounting for over 70 percent of the world's total. Its expressway network extends to nearly 200,000 kilometers, the largest in the world.
The transformation is particularly visible in Guizhou, where rugged karst terrain long made travel difficult. More than 32,000 bridges have been completed or are under construction in the province, including the Huajiang Grand Canyon Bridge, the world's highest bridge.
Communities along the historic route have also changed. In Guangxi's Quanzhou, Guanyang and Xing'an counties, where the Battle of the Xiangjiang River was fought, more than 100 formerly impoverished villages have been lifted out of poverty through targeted poverty alleviation efforts.
Despite China's profound transformation over recent decades, new challenges remain on its path toward Chinese modernization.
Wan Laizhi, a scholar of CPC history at Guangxi Normal University, said retracing the Long March route helps people appreciate how earlier generations faced adversity and held to their convictions, drawing strength and inspiration from their example to overcome challenges facing China today.
Chen Lipeng, a professor at Renmin University of China, said retracing the route can also help promote tourism in former revolutionary areas and support rural revitalization.
Interest in revolutionary heritage sites is growing, particularly among younger visitors. In the first half of 2026, interest in booking tickets for such attractions rose 86 percent year on year, while bookings by people aged 18 to 35 accounted for more than half of the total, according to industry data.
Luo and Ding, for their part, have worked to keep that history alive. Back home in Zunyi City, they compiled their experiences into books and began visiting schools to share what they had learned.
Earlier this year, they opened a homestay in their village, employing more than 10 local residents. Luo plans to turn part of it into a small educational site displaying materials collected during their journeys.
"Young people today may not face the hardships people endured in the past, but everyone encounters difficulties in life," he said. "I want them to know that there is always a way forward. That is what the Long March spirit means to me."
(Reporting by Cheng Lu, Bai Xu, Wang Jian, Rong Jiaojiao, Li Jingya, Shi Qiangui and Guo Yifan; Video reporters: Liu Qinbing, Zhao Yingbo and Yao Youming; Video editors: Hong Ling, Zhang Mocheng and Zheng Xin.) ■

articles.title_orig: El Salvador president says bodies found in Haiti are not those of hostages
articles.title_zh: El Salvador president says bodies found in Haiti are not those of hostages
articles.content_orig:
Four bodies handed over to special forces on a mission to Haiti to recover Salvadoran hostages are "not our men", El Salvador's president has said.
Nayib Bukele said a nongovernmental organisation delivered the human remains to one of Haiti's airports claiming they were four El Salvadoran air technicians, but that one of the corpses was a child's and another was wearing a different country's army uniform.
He had dispatched a military contingent, reportedly of hundreds of soldiers, on Thursday after the four men vanished after being ambushed by "heavily armed criminal groups".
The hostages had been part of the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF), which is tasked with tackling worsening gang violence in Haiti.
The men had been travelling back to their camp in an armoured vehicle when they were attacked in an area of the Caribbean island nation controlled by armed groups called Croix-des-Bouquets. No gang has so far claimed responsibility.
Bukele previously said the Salvadoran military operation in Haiti had the sole purpose of returning the four men alive. Approximately 450 soldiers had so far been deployed, according to Haitian newspaper Le Nouvelliste.
Bukele said the bodies the mission had received included one of a man of "considerably greater height than that of our air technicians", a person "who was wearing part of a uniform from an army that is not ours", and that among the remains were identification cards and uniforms from other countries.
He posted pictures showing the ID card of a GSF member and a corresponding national ID card from Chad in Africa.
Bukele's comments poured skepticism on an earlier report in the New York Times, citing people close to the Salvadoran mission, that the bodies found on the outskirts of the Haitian capital, Port-au-Prince, on Saturday were thought to belong to the missing men.
The newspaper reported that the bodies delivered to the military contingent had been badly burned, meaning a medical examination would be required to identify them.
It cited one unnamed source briefed on the situation as saying the ID posted by Bukele in fact belonged to a soldier who had lost it when he had been injured.
Haiti has been ravaged by gang violence for years, but the situation has worsened in the political vacuum that followed the assassination of its president in 2021.
The multinational force dispatched to quell the violence and push back the armed gangs has struggled to penetrate areas where they hold sway.
More than 5,700 people have been killed or injured by gangs or during operations against them between 1 January and 11 September this year, the UN said at the start of October.
Bukele said the four GSF members had primarily been there to "carry out medical evacuations and save lives, not to wage war".
When they were abducted, helicopters were deployed and multiple attempts were made to reach the location, but these efforts were hampered by fighting in the area, the Salvadoran armed forces said.

articles.title_orig: More than 1,300 arrested as clashes follow another day of mass protests across France
articles.title_zh: More than 1,300 arrested as clashes follow another day of mass protests across France
articles.content_orig:
More than 1,300 arrests were made as hundreds of thousands of people took part in another day of protests across France on Saturday that were followed by some clashes later in the day, officials have said.
After largely peaceful demonstrations, police fired tear gas and water cannon to disperse protesters in a number of cities including Paris, while barricades were set alight in Marseille and people ripped boards from a shop in Bordeaux.
Officials have so far managed to avoid rioting and looting on the scale seen last weekend, which resulted in some of the worst scenes of disorder in France's modern history.
The interior ministry said an estimated 410,000 people protested on Saturday, while the unions put the number at about 800,000.
Some 70,000 police officers were deployed and restrictions imposed in several cities to prevent the latest protests over the cost of living and poor school conditions from descending into the kind of chaos which saw officers outnumbered, hundreds of businesses looted and buildings torched.
The interior ministry said 53 officers were hurt in clashes across the country on Saturday.
French President Emmanuel Macron had decreed earlier this week that only demonstrations organised by a recognised trade unions would be permitted. Hundreds of people have been jailed for vandalism, arson and looting after fast-track court hearings.
Clashes between protesters and riot police in Paris erupted at the end of a peaceful march from the city's Porte d'Italie towards Porte de Vincennes, where the police operation included an elite unit that usually deals with organised crime and counter-terrorism.
Some protesters were seen erecting makeshift barricades and pelting officers with projectiles, while police baton-charged groups of masked youths who were smashing the windows of a car dealership.
French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said that "several thousand radical activists gathered at the rear of the march, including around 500 individuals identified as rioters", news agency AFP reported.
The Interior Ministry said 142 people were arrested in the French capital on Saturday, less than half of the number arrested on the same day last week.
In the southern port of Marseille, rubbish bins were set ablaze and metal sheets used to block streets. A law enforcement vehicle was seen driving through a burning barricade in France's second-largest city.
Meanwhile, some protesters in dark clothing and face coverings were seen taking boards off a building to build a street barricade in the southern city of Bordeaux.
In Lyon, police used tear gas grenades to disperse a crowd which had reportedly gathered in an area deemed off-limits by the local prefecture.
"There were around 150 of us, mostly secondary school and university students. Then the tear gas came almost immediately. You could barely see anything in the street," said one protester in France's third-largest city.
Nuñez also said two people had been "seriously injured": one in the south-western city of Toulouse and another one in Clermont-Ferrand, central France. He said the number of arrests across the country would likely rise.
The man in Toulouse, a 20-year-old protester, had several fingers torn off one hand when a nearby explosive went off, Franceinfo reported, citing the medic who treated him.
As the unrest continued into the early hours of Sunday morning, authorities in Bouches-du-Rhône, the region in which Marseilles sits, said seven businesses had been "looted or damaged".
Earlier, a peaceful protester in Paris who gave her name as Zelie told the BBC people had taken to the streets because they were "really frustrated" and had been "suffering a lot" since Macron came to office.
"They keep us quiet. They take our money, they tax us a lot and we can't say anything. Today we are in the streets because it's been too long, it's been too much," the 26-year-old said.
Two masked teenage protesters, who did not want to give their names, also said their generation was in despair and felt abandoned by the government.
"I think looting is really not good," one of the demonstrators said of last Saturday's disorder. "But it's because of poverty and the violence of the police."
He added that the protests would end "when we have a response to our demands. We really want a change in France".
Meanwhile, some 13,000 people joined a rally against the hard-right National Rally (RN) party in the north-central city of Orléans, which proceeded peacefully.
The recent unrest has played out against a backdrop of a polarised political landscape, with France preparing for what could be the most divisive election period in a generation.
Macron will leave office next spring and polls suggest French voters will ultimately face a choice between RN's candidate Marine Le Pen and that of the radical-left La France Insoumise (France Unbowed).
Leading figures from both parties have levelled the blame for the disorder at Macron, though right-wing figures have also heaped criticism on rioters while left-wing leaders support the union-led protests.
LFI candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon said French media had not covered the peaceful protests while police had created "a setup deliberately designed to provoke chaos" that had "mutilated two people".
Mass protests triggered by similar issues as in France also rocked several other European cities on Saturday.
In Barcelona, more than 120 people were arrested after a student protest descended into what local authorities described as "gratuitous violence".
In Albania's capital Tirana, riot police fired tear gas to disperse thousands of anti-government demonstrators, while clashes were also reported in Belgium's capital Brussels.
In Milan, northern Italy, a major security operation including hundreds of soldiers alongside police prevented protesters gathering in the city. Many had feared a repeat of violent scenes last week when some started fires, smashed windows and looted shops.
Around 550,000 people took part in last weekend's demonstrations against rising fuel prices and the cost of living, with frustrations escalating after weeks of student protests. The chaos which followed resulted in more than 2,500 arrests.
Marches were initially largely peaceful but became marred by scenes of violence, looting and destruction, with more than 2,000 shops and other businesses across France said to have been directly impacted. The damage was estimated "at hundreds of millions euros", France's Chambers of Commerce and Industry (CCI) said.
One demonstrator's hand was blown off by a police crowd-control grenade, according to AFP, while about 1,000 police officers were injured.
The French authorities later said they were forced to impose overnight curfews in Paris and other cities.
The continuing protests come ahead of France's presidential elections in six months' time, and leading contenders have levelled the blame at Macron and his ministers.

articles.title_orig: Former Israeli army chief Gadi Eisenkot emerges as Netanyahu’s leading election challenger
articles.title_zh: Former Israeli army chief Gadi Eisenkot emerges as Netanyahu’s leading election challenger
articles.content_orig:
Fox News Digital speaks with three experts on Israel’s high-stakes election and the fight over Netanyahu’s political future. The election is set for Oct. 27, 2026.
JERUSALEM — Israel’s high-stakes election on Oct. 27 pits the longest serving prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, against the highly decorated retired Lt. Gen. Gadi Eisenkot. While fairly new to politics, Eisenkot has an impressive resume that could help him become the Jewish state's next leader.
According to a number of polls, Eisenkot's centrist political party, Yashar, has a narrow lead over Netanyahu's Likud. To form a government, Yashar or Likud will need to cobble together a 61-seat majority of parties to be able to form a new coalition government.
TRUMP SAYS NETANYAHU NEEDS TO BE RE-ELECTED, OR ELSE US WILL HAVE TO 'FINISH THE JOB’ AGAINST IRAN ALONE
Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party, speaks from behind a podium with a banner reading "Yashar with Eisenkot" during an event presenting the party's full candidate list ahead of October's general election on Sept. 7, 2026 in Rosh HaAyin, Israel. Eisenkot, a retired chief of the Israel Defense Forces, has emerged as the foremost challenger to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. (Erik Marmor/Getty Images)
He was born in Tiberias in Israel’s north to a Jewish-Moroccan family who relocated to Israel’s southernmost city, Eilat, on the Red Sea when he was a toddler.
A career soldier, he opted to serve in the infantry. He was part of the elite Golani Brigade and reached the zenith of the military with his 2015 appointment to the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) chief of staff in 2015 until 2019.
Yossi Melman, one of Israel’s most respected journalists on intelligence and defense reporting, told Fox News Digital that Eisenkot, "Is 100% a soldier. He is very brave and humble. He is an officer and gentleman."
Melman noted that when Eisenkot was chosen to be the next IDF chief of staff, he declined because he felt that then General Benny Gantz should receive the appointment. Melman asked, "How many people would do that? He was selected after Gantz. It shows his traits of modesty, honesty and not arrogant."
Melman said, "It is a miracle he is leading in the polls. He is the antithesis of a what a politician should be. He is not a great orator when you compare him to Netanyahu. He radiates honesty."
BENJAMIN NETANYAHU'S LEGACY AND POLITICAL FUTURE ON THE LINE IN ISRAEL'S OCT 27 ELECTION
Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot attends the Jerusalem Residents Conference on Aug. 12, 2026 in Jerusalem. Gadi Eisenkot, a retired chief of the Israel Defense Forces and current leader of the Yashar party, has emerged as the foremost challenger to Benjamin Netanyahu ahead of October's general election. (Erik Marmor/Getty Images)
Eisenkot’s Mizrahi background — Jews who originate from North Africa and the Middle East — would mean, if he prevails, that he would be the first Israeli Prime Minister of Moroccan origin. The Prime Minister’s office has been held by Israelis of Eastern European descent (Ashkenazi) since the rebirth of the Jewish state in 1948.
After Hamas invaded Israel on Oct. 7, 2023 and slaughtered over 1,200 people, including more than 40 Americans, Eisenkot joined Netanyahu’s war cabinet as a minister without portfolio.
Melman said Eisenkot "did not set any political conditions" and "his presence in the cabinet saved Netanyahu." After eight months of serving in the war cabinet, Eisenkot resigned, blaming the prime minister for failing to implement a comprehensive strategy.
The war against the Iran-backed terrorist movement Hamas took an enormous toll on the battle-hardened General Eisenkot and his family. Hamas killed his son, 25-year-old Master Sergeant Gal Eisenkot, in Dec. 2023. The terrorist organization also killed two nephews of Eisenkot. Netanyahu and his wife Sara said at the time that they were devastated by Gal’s death and Eisenkot was a "true hero."
ZIONISM EXPLAINED FROM ITS BIBLICAL ORIGINS TO THE REBIRTH OF THE STATE OF ISRAEL
Gadi Eisenkot, former Israeli army chief of staff and head of the Yashar party, is seen at the Black Arrow memorial site near Kibbutz Mefalsim during a visit to deliver a statement near the border with the Gaza Strip on Oct. 15, 2026, ahead of the Israel's legislative election. (Ilia Yefimovich/AFP via Getty Images)
Danny Orbach, a military historian from the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, gave his take on the leading contender to replace Netanyahu. "I think his military record and his prospects as a national leader have both significant strengths and serious weaknesses. He bears considerable responsibility for shaping the IDF that existed on Oct. 7, 2023. And that was, paradoxically, both the army that proved capable of defeating Hezbollah, striking Iran and achieving unprecedented military successes in the extraordinarily difficult, tunnel-ridden battlefield of Gaza and the army that failed so miserably on Oct. 7."
He continued that, "Like other chiefs of staff, Eisenkot bears responsibility for the decisions that reduced the army's size and for the infamous ‘conceptzia’ [Hebrew word for concept] regarding Hamas. In that respect, I consider him just as culpable as Netanyahu."
Israel’s military, intelligence and political establishments bought into the ‘conceptzia’ that Hamas could be housebroken with massive infusions of economic aid. Hamas, however, was wedded to its radical Islamist ideology —the destruction of the Jewish state — and used the funds to advance its war aims.
Orbach noted that "I don't think most of Eisenkot's support stems from his energy, enthusiasm or even his political platform. My impression is that Eisenkot has emerged as the default ‘non-Bibi’ candidate, the politician who currently channels much of the camp's hopes and expectations."
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Israeli Chief of Staff Gadi Eizenkot (L) give a press conference in Tel Aviv, on Dec. 4, 2018. Israel's army said today it has discovered Hezbollah tunnels infiltrating its territory from Lebanon and launched an operation to destroy them, a move likely to raise tensions with the Iran-backed group. (Jack Guez/AFP Via Getty Images)
Orbach added that "I also doubt that Eisenkot would have had the political determination to stand up to the Biden administration on such matters."
Netanyahu and former President Biden repeatedly clashed over Biden’s attempts to rope in Israel’s efforts to defeat Iran’s seven-front war against the Jewish state.
The military historian, however, noted that "I believe an Eisenkot government could address several of Israel's most urgent problems. It would remove Ben Gvir from power, confront the growing problem of Jewish extremist violence and terrorism in the West Bank, and begin repairing Israel's severely damaged international legitimacy."
Itamar Ben-Gvir is a controversial right-wing firebrand politician and the current minister of national security since 2022, who has outraged many Western European and foreign leaders with his heated rhetoric against the Palestinians.
TIMELINE OF DECADES-LONG ISRAELI-ARAB, PALESTINIAN CONFLICT
Former army chief Gadi Eisenkot attends the funeral for his son, First Sergeant Major Gal Meir Eisenkot, 25 years old, at the Herzliya cemetery on Dec. 8, 2023 in Herzliya, Israel. The Israel Defense Forces said the 25-year-old major, son of the cabinet minister and former army chief Gadi Eisenkot, died on Thursday in Gaza. (Dima Vazinovich / Middle East Images / Middle East Images/AFP via Getty Images))
Eisenkot’s wife, Hannah, comes from an American Jewish family. U.S. General Joseph Dunford awarded Eisenkot the Commander of the Legion of Merit because of his "exceptionally meritorious service as chief of the General Staff of the IDF" and his "contribution to the strategic cooperation between the United States and Israel [that] will have a lasting effect on both countries," according to the Washington Institute, where Eisenkot served as a military fellow in 2019

articles.title_orig: GeForce Unlocked: Modders Boost RTX 20, RTX 30, and RTX 40 Compute Performance by Up to 2x
articles.title_zh: GeForce Unlocked: Modders Boost RTX 20, RTX 30, and RTX 40 Compute Performance by Up to 2x
articles.content_orig:
The new tool reportedly helps the RTX 3090 Ti's BF16 compute performance jump from 87.5 FLOPS to 157 TFLOPS while also improving the vLLM inference speeds by up to 36%.
A new trick has been unlocked to bypass NVIDIA's software-level restrictions on consumer GeForce graphics cards. This has been achieved with a new open-source project called "GPU Unlock", which allows the GPUs to access higher half-precision floating-point compute performance, which typically is reserved for the professional workstation GPUs.
According to the project's developer, "zagitta", NVIDIA restricts certain compute capabilities and virtual GPU (vGPU) features on consumer GeForce GPUs, despite sharing the same GPU architecture as the professional workstation cards. NVIDIA restricts these capabilities to the more expensive Quadra, Testa and RTX A-series GPUs. However, this new project takes a different approach from traditional driver.
"GPU Unlock" dynamically patches the NVIDIA driver module within the Linux kernel and intercepts requests for the GPU's physical PCIe Device ID before replacing the returned identifier with that of a compatible professional GPU. This basically tricks the driver into recognizing a consumer GeForce GPU as a professional NVIDIA card, bypassing the restrictions and unlocking additional compute capabilities.
As per the developer's claims, the performance improvements are substantial. On the GeForce RTX 3090 Ti, an Ampere GPU, the BF16 compute performance increases from 87.5 TFLOPS to a whopping 157 TFLOPS , which is a staggering 80% improvement. The TF32 performance also nearly doubles, rising from 42.6 TFLOPS to 82.6 TFLOPS. The GeForce RTX 3080 reportedly also benefits from this, and its FP16/BF16 performance increases from 65 TFLOPS to 110-113 TFLOPS , while retaining its default 320W power limit.
The benefits were also seen in the vLLM inference engine, where the tool unlocks 33-36% additional performance in long-context Prefill processing speeds and a 25% reduction in Time-To-First-Token latency. However, Decode performance remained mostly unchanged because the technique doesn't address memory bandwidth limitations.
That said, the GPU Unlock currently supports Linux only and works with GeForce GTX 900, GTX 1000, RTX 20, and RTX 30 series GPUs, while the RTX 40 and RTX 50 cards aren't supported.

Sarfraz's hands-on experience is demonstrated through his first-person accounts of using and comparing different hardware configurations, providing practical and relatable insights for everyday users. His technical analysis is respected by peers in the enthusiast community and has been cited by specialized hardware sites such as Germany's Igor's Lab.

articles.title_orig: Israeli elections: What are the possible outcomes?
articles.title_zh: Israeli elections: What are the possible outcomes?
articles.content_orig:
Israel is heading to the polls on October 27 in an election that could end Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s long grip on power.
The vote for all 120 seats in the Knesset is the first since the Hamas-led attacks of October 7, 2023, the onset of Israel’s subsequent genocidal war on Gaza and a wider conflict that has seen Israel carry out attacks in several countries across the region.
Opinion polls suggest his right-wing bloc is in a close race against a Jewish-led opposition alliance. But defeating Netanyahu at the ballot box does not necessarily mean removing him from power.
Israel’s proportional representation system means parties must negotiate alliances to secure a governing majority in the Knesset. No single party has ever won an outright majority of at least 61 seats.
According to recent polling, the opposition bloc is projected to win 52 seats, compared with 50 for Netanyahu’s religious-nationalist alliance. Palestinian-led parties could, therefore, determine who governs.
Here are eight possible outcomes:
Despite slightly trailing in opinion polls, Netanyahu could remain prime minister if his Likud party assembles enough parliamentary support from existing allies or new coalition partners.
His traditional partners include far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir’s Jewish Power party and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionism party.
Ultra-Orthodox parties Shas and United Torah Judaism – which have previously joined his coalition multiple times but also walked away, most recently in 2025 – could also play an important role.
In late September, four opposition parties signed a non-aggression pact, agreeing to work together in a bid to unseat Netanyahu.
The rival movements – the Yashar party, the Democrats, the Yisrael Beytenu party and the Together alliance – said they are united in their goal to “preserve and strengthen Israel as a Jewish and democratic state”.
The bloc has not announced who would lead a future governing coalition, but former army chief Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party, is seen as its most likely prime ministerial candidate.
Former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, who heads the Together alliance with Yair Lapid, is another potential candidate.
The Joint List and Ra’am – the two Arab-led parties representing the Palestinian citizens of Israel, who make up about 20 percent of the population – are projected to win about 13 seats.
Ra’am, also known as the United Arab List, made history in 2021 by joining Bennett’s coalition, becoming the first Arab-led party to participate in an Israeli governing coalition.
Mansour Abbas , leader of Ra’am, has signalled a willingness to repeat that arrangement if the opposition-led alliance needs additional seats.
He has said his priorities include combatting the wave of violent crime that has been allowed to engulf Palestinian communities, as well as addressing discriminatory government policies, including on housing.
However, most opposition leaders, including Eisenkot, have ruled out such an alliance.
If a coalition falls short of 61 seats, it could seek outside parliamentary support from other parties without including them in government, such as the Palestinian-led parties.
Joint List, which includes the Hadash, Ta’al and Balad factions, has said it could provide a so-called safety net to the anti-Netanyahu coalition by agreeing not to stand against it in a confidence vote, even if the alliance does not join the government. In return, it has said it would demand certain conditions, including a path to Palestinian statehood and fighting organised crime.
However, any such arrangement would leave the governing coalition vulnerable to defections and disputes over major policies.
A national unity government, according to Israel’s parliament, is a “government based on a broad coalition, the members of which also include representatives of rival parliamentary groups”.
This is usually formed at times of national emergencies, such as war, natural disasters or economic crises.
In May 2020, Netanyahu and Benny Gantz formed a unity government following three inconclusive elections. That agreement collapsed within a year.
However, in 2023, following the Hamas-led attacks on Israel, Gantz and members of his party joined Netanyahu’s coalition – seen as an emergency unity government – despite Gantz previously bitterly opposing it.
Two political leaders could agree to alternate as prime minister under a power-sharing arrangement.
Netanyahu and Gantz agreed to such a rotation in 2020, but their coalition collapsed before Gantz could take over.
Bennett and Lapid made the same arrangement for the prime minister’s office to change hands after the former came into power in June 2021. After Bennett’s coalition lost its parliamentary majority in June 2022, Lapid took over as caretaker prime minister in July that year.
In Israel, the prime minister is voted in by members of the Knesset after an election.
If negotiations stall over forming a government, parties could agree to support another Knesset member from Netanyahu’s political camp or that of an opposition bloc, someone who is more acceptable to future partners.
If no leader can assemble sufficient support in the Knesset, Israel could face another period of political turbulence and head for a new election.
The country held five elections between 2019 and 2022 as rival blocs repeatedly struggled to form stable governments.
In such a scenario, Netanyahu would remain caretaker prime minister until a new administration took office.

articles.title_orig: Houthis launch attacks on Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Aden
articles.title_zh: Houthis launch attacks on Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Aden
articles.content_orig:
Houthi fighters have launched a series of attacks on targets in Saudi Arabia and the seat of Yemen’s internationally recognised government in Aden, while the fighting intensifies around the city of Taiz.
In a Facebook post on Saturday, the Yemeni government’s Ministry of Transport denounced what it described as the Houthis’ targeting of Aden international airport with two ballistic missiles, calling it the “fourth such attack this month”.
The airport attacks pose “a threat to the safety of civil aviation” and have “humanitarian and economic repercussions for citizens” who rely on it, the ministry warned.
Yemeni authorities said the coastguard headquarters and a second building were also hit.
The Houthis claimed attacks on the al-Nasr camp and Aden’s naval military base.
Yemen’s army said a Houthi missile killed three people when it malfunctioned and fell on a family home in Houthi-held Sanaa on Friday. The army said it was one of several missile malfunctions seen in recent weeks by the Iran-backed group.
Houthi-run Al Masirah TV said on Saturday that Saudi-led coalition air attacks killed several civilians in the capital, Sanaa, and in the port city of Hodeidah. The claim could not be verified and Saudi Arabia has not commented on the alleged raids.
The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said on Sunday that it downed a ballistic missile launched by the Houthis towards the Saudi capital, Riyadh.
“Air defences intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the terrorist Houthi militia toward Riyadh,” the coalition’s spokesperson said in a social media post.
On Saturday, Saudi Arabia’s civil defence said on X the Houthis had launched two ballistic missiles towards Mecca and Medina, warning of “the fall of shrapnel” following their interception.
Images shared on X by the Saudi Press Agency appeared to show a large, blackened missile-shaped object that had landed somewhere in Saudi Arabia.
Jasem Mohamed Albudaiwi, secretary-general of the Gulf Cooperation Council, described the Houthi attacks as “heinous” and said they embodied “a blatant disregard for the lives and security of civilians” in a statement shared on Saturday.
The Houthis said the claim that they targeted the two cities – the holiest in Islam – was a “huge lie”. They said their targets were three Saudi airports, oil infrastructure and an airbase.
The Houthis have persistently targeted Saudi energy infrastructure and airports across the country with long-range strikes since a fragile ceasefire agreed in 2022 fell apart in July .
Riyadh’s international airport said in a social media post on Saturday that flights would resume on Sunday after a two-week closure following Houthi strikes on the capital.
Shortly after the announcement, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree issued a warning on X, saying the airport is still “unsafe” and remains a “military target”.
The Flightradar24 monitoring site showed a plane taking off from Riyadh airport early on Sunday, heading to the Saudi city of Jeddah.
Intense fighting is continuing on Yemen’s front lines as the Houthis battle forces of the internationally recognised government for control of key areas.
On Saturday, Yemeni army spokesman Colonel Majed Abdullah al-Nazili said government forces had carried out more than 700 “targeting operations” over the last 24 hours across Yemen, “neutralising” 300 Houthi fighters and disabling military vehicles.
Al Jazeera could not independently verify those figures.
Operations targeted field command centres, Houthi gatherings, weapons depots, and supply lines in Taiz, where intense clashes have been ongoing for days, the spokesman added.
The Houthis have been launching attacks on the western, eastern and southern fronts of Taiz, with attempts by Houthi fighters to break through and advance from the western front towards the city of Taiz in an effort to capture it, Al Jazeera correspondent Hadeel al-Yamani reported on Saturday.
Government forces, supported by fighters from the Popular Resistance group, have pushed back against Houthi attacks to break through from the eastern front.

articles.title_orig: Apple Wants to Fix Safari's Cramped Layout on iPhone Duo
articles.title_zh: Apple Wants to Fix Safari's Cramped Layout on iPhone Duo
articles.content_orig:
Apple is considering changes to Safari on the iPhone Duo that would give websites access to more of the outer display, although the company has yet to settle on an approach.
The challenge is allowing pages to occupy the area beneath Safari's side-mounted controls without making parts of a website inaccessible. In an Friday, October 23 WebKit post , Apple's Jen Simmons explained that an existing web setting could enable this, but Apple's research suggests many sites would not handle it correctly.
That setting, viewport-fit="cover", allows a webpage to expand into areas that would otherwise be reserved. Website developers must then leave enough space around important content to prevent it from being covered by the interface. According to Simmons, many sites fail to make those allowances on every edge.
Apple is investigating whether another solution could offer developers more control with less risk of obscuring content. A header's background could, for example, span the screen while its navigation links remain within the unobstructed portion.
For now, Safari 27.1 restricts webpages to the area beside the controls and uses the page's background color to fill the remaining strip. This limits the width available for content on the outer display.
The arrangement stems from the screen's proportions. Apple placed controls along the side of the device because the outer display is shorter and wider than other iPhone screens, preserving more height for apps and webpages.
Separately, Safari 27.1 adds automatic two-page PDF viewing when the ‌iPhone Duo‌ is held partially folded like a book. Flattening or closing the device returns the document to a single-page view.
Developers can also test experimental support for detecting the screen's folding posture and positioning content around the device's middle fold. Those features are available behind Safari feature flags, while the proposed change to content beneath the controls remains under investigation.

articles.title_orig: Which AMD CPU Is Equivalent To The One In The PlayStation 5 Pro?
articles.title_zh: Which AMD CPU Is Equivalent To The One In The PlayStation 5 Pro?
articles.content_orig:
The PlayStation 5 Pro is the most powerful console on the market. Not only does it have more blazing hardware that allows gamers to experience the latest games at high resolutions and framerates, but it also comes with special features like PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution to further enhance visual clarity.
Building a PC that matches the PS5 Pro is tough since the console has a fully custom set of AMD hardware inside, but there are definitely similar components you can buy if you know what to look for. The closest AMD CPU match to the PS5 Pro is the Ryzen 5 5600x, which can keep pace with the PS5 Pro's framerates in most games. It's not a one-to-one comparison since the PS5 Pro has a fully custom processor designed to handle different things, but the Ryzen 5 5600x can keep up with the Pro and drive games past 60 Frames Per Second (FPS) with a compatible display.
The AMD Ryzen 5 5600X delivers nearly identical performance to the PS5 Pro in most scenarios. Most of the PS5 Pro's benefits come from graphical improvements that would be handled by a dedicated GPU on a PC, so it doesn't actually take a top-of-the-line CPU to keep up with Sony's flagship console.
Cyberpunk 2077 is the best example of this. Now that the game has a dedicated PS5 Pro patch with an unlocked framerate and boosted graphics, both processors can be tested under intense loads. On PS5 Pro, for example, Digital Foundry found that Cyberpunk 2077 can reach as high as 90 FPS in performance mode, but the framerate dips in heavy-use scenarios. You can see nearly identical benchmarks with the 5600X on PC, averaging just below 90 FPS and dipping down to 60 as a worst-case scenario in ProYamYamPC's testing .
The comparison still holds up with ray tracing enabled. There are multiple ray tracing modes in the PS5 Pro version of Cyberpunk 2077, but the primary one enables most ray tracing enhancements while keeping the frame rate locked at 60. ProYamYamPC found that the Ryzen 5 5600X can maintain an average of 60 FPS with ray tracing set to Ultra. Ray tracing performance will largely depend on your graphics card, but the 5600X won't be a bottleneck in a PC equivalent to the PS5 Pro .
Of course, there are high-end options that can outperform the PS5 Pro if you're willing to spend some extra cash. With the PS5 Pro's price hike to $900 , however, these expensive CPUs are becoming a much more attractive option for gamers looking to upgrade.
The Ryzen 7 9800X3D is one of the best gaming CPUs on the market, and it easily outclasses the PS5 Pro in most games. Looking at Control Resonant, the PS5 Pro and Ryzen 5 5600X run at 60 FPS with frequent dips in heavy scenarios. The Ryzen 7 9800X3D, meanwhile, can reach triple-digit framerates in the same scenes, according to benchmarks run by Testing Games .
Even less expensive AMD CPUs like the Ryzen 7 7700X3D — priced at $329 compared to $479 for the 9800X3D — outperform the PS5 Pro. Taking another look at Cyberpunk 2077, Digital Foundry testing shows that the 7700X3D averages over 100 FPS in most areas and only dips as low as 90 FPS in crowded scenes. That's better than the PS5 Pro's performance mode, and you'll be able to maintain those framerates with advanced graphical settings if you have a PS5 Pro equivalent GPU or better.

articles.title_orig: Remains Found in Haiti During Hunt for Missing Salvadoran Soldiers
articles.title_zh: Remains Found in Haiti During Hunt for Missing Salvadoran Soldiers
articles.content_orig:
Four bodies handed over to special forces on a mission to Haiti to recover Salvadoran hostages are "not our men", El Salvador's president has said.
Nayib Bukele said a nongovernmental organisation delivered the human remains to one of Haiti's airports claiming they were four El Salvadoran air technicians, but that one of the corpses was a child's and another was wearing a different country's army uniform.
He had dispatched a military contingent, reportedly of hundreds of soldiers, on Thursday after the four men vanished after being ambushed by "heavily armed criminal groups".
The hostages had been part of the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF), which is tasked with tackling worsening gang violence in Haiti.
The men had been travelling back to their camp in an armoured vehicle when they were attacked in an area of the Caribbean island nation controlled by armed groups called Croix-des-Bouquets. No gang has so far claimed responsibility.
Bukele previously said the Salvadoran military operation in Haiti had the sole purpose of returning the four men alive. Approximately 450 soldiers had so far been deployed, according to Haitian newspaper Le Nouvelliste.
Bukele said the bodies the mission had received included one of a man of "considerably greater height than that of our air technicians", a person "who was wearing part of a uniform from an army that is not ours", and that among the remains were identification cards and uniforms from other countries.
He posted pictures showing the ID card of a GSF member and a corresponding national ID card from Chad in Africa.
Bukele's comments poured skepticism on an earlier report in the New York Times, citing people close to the Salvadoran mission, that the bodies found on the outskirts of the Haitian capital, Port-au-Prince, on Saturday were thought to belong to the missing men.
The newspaper reported that the bodies delivered to the military contingent had been badly burned, meaning a medical examination would be required to identify them.
It cited one unnamed source briefed on the situation as saying the ID posted by Bukele in fact belonged to a soldier who had lost it when he had been injured.
Haiti has been ravaged by gang violence for years, but the situation has worsened in the political vacuum that followed the assassination of its president in 2021.
The multinational force dispatched to quell the violence and push back the armed gangs has struggled to penetrate areas where they hold sway.
More than 5,700 people have been killed or injured by gangs or during operations against them between 1 January and 11 September this year, the UN said at the start of October.
Bukele said the four GSF members had primarily been there to "carry out medical evacuations and save lives, not to wage war".
When they were abducted, helicopters were deployed and multiple attempts were made to reach the location, but these efforts were hampered by fighting in the area, the Salvadoran armed forces said.

articles.title_orig: China's clean energy achievements accelerate global energy transition, says IEA chief
articles.title_zh: China's clean energy achievements accelerate global energy transition, says IEA chief
articles.content_orig:
Power lines near the Gravelines Nuclear Power Station in Gravelines, France on Sept. 15
Recent weeks have brought red flag after red flag for investment in AI and the related data center boom. Bond yields soared for AI infrastructure giant CoreWeave, a sign that investors view the buildout as increasingly risky. And Meta’s reporting of negative free cash flow for the quarter to fund its infrastructure buildout while saying it might need to raise even more capital to fund its AI buildout not only hit its own stock but contributed to a price decline across the big tech companies.
These developments raised questions across Wall Street about whether too much is being spent too quickly on data center expansion. How questions over data center investment play out has big implications for how companies and investors approach the future of energy and, by extension, climate . A pullback in the pace of new data centers could ease pressure to build fossil generation, but it would also weaken the commercial case for clean energy technologies that need big, reliable buyers who are willing to pay a premium for power.
Most obviously, a dent in the AI buildout would translate directly into a slowdown in related electricity demand growth. In advanced economies like the U.S., data centers will account for 20% of that growth through 2030. By then, data centers are expected to account for 3% of global electricity demand, according to data from the International Energy Agency.
Making sense of the climate and energy economy.
Some climate advocates may initially rejoice at slowing electricity demand. Even as renewable energy expands, grids around the world still rely on fossil fuels. In the U.S. in particular, AI demand has sparked a wave of building new natural gas infrastructure. In the short term, slowing demand would mean lower emissions from the existing system than today’s baseline assumptions and less investment in new natural gas infrastructure.
But a slowing data center build out leaves less mature technologies at risk. From advanced geothermal to new ways of producing nuclear power, big tech companies have been willing to pay more to lock in reliable power sources, thereby accelerating the market for these new efforts. Even unproven technologies like nuclear fusion have received a big financial boost from tech firms speculating that they might help solve their power challenges and give them a competitive leg up in the AI race. In a tighter financial environment with lower projected electricity demand, both the incentive and the financial capacity to make bold bets diminish.
To be clear, data centers are not the only source of growing electricity demand. New manufacturing continues to create the need for power. The need for air conditioning has ramped up in many emerging markets, particularly in the Global South, creating new grid pressures. And electric vehicles continue to take off in many markets outside the U.S.
Even as gas remains resilient, much of the power built to meet demand will come from clean sources, including and especially solar and battery storage. Solar is increasingly cost competitive. And this year’s spike in fuel prices—particularly natural gas—has made local power more appealing. But the companies behind growing sectors like air conditioning and EVs are less involved in local power systems and lack the capital to really shape them like the world’s wealthiest tech companies have. In short, clean energy will take a hit without the backing of big tech.
It’s too soon to tell whether, in the long run, this week’s AI infrastructure recalibration will be a blip in time or part of a much broader realignment. But it’s something that anyone invested in clean energy and climate should be watching closely.

articles.title_orig: Iranians Face Anxious Wait as Threat of Attack Looms
articles.title_zh: Iranians Face Anxious Wait as Threat of Attack Looms
articles.content_orig:
Escalating war rhetoric from Iran, the United States and Israel, coupled with military movements across the region, has heightened fears of another conflict, as Iranians debate online whether war could bring political change or deepen the country's crises.
Iranian social media users are closely following statements by US President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, as well as diplomatic and military movements across the region.
Many view the developments as possible signs of an impending US-Israeli attack.
A central debate is whether another war could bring down the Islamic Republic or simply inflict further damage on Iran.
Those supporting military action describe war as a necessary evil to end the political system, arguing that previous attempts to bring about change have failed.
Opponents warn that another conflict could destroy energy infrastructure and refineries, deepen economic hardship and leave Iranian society in an even worse position.
“We are inside Iran and face all kinds of financial, security and social problems, but we are willing to pay the price to end this nightmare,” one user wrote.
Another user wrote: “This uncertainty is really a thousand times worse than war. We cannot even plan a trip, let alone make decisions about work, education or running a business.”
Others strongly rejected that view.
“War brings destruction, chaos, disease and so many other problems,” one user wrote. “The outcome will not necessarily be what you imagine. It could be much worse than things are now.”
Another highlighted the vulnerability of people without secure salaries, who could lose their livelihoods if fighting disrupted economic activity.
One user summed up the conflicting attitudes they had encountered.
“I have seen many people in Iran waiting for an attack so that things can finally be settled… and others who wanted an agreement to be reached,” the user wrote. “Feelings differ, but everyone is tired of this situation.”
Some are urging others to stock up on water, food and medicine and keep cash on hand. Others warn people living near military or government facilities to consider leaving.
Users have also expressed concern for elderly people, those with illnesses and people living alone.
Hardliners push for confrontation
Ultra-hardline voices have also expressed enthusiasm for military confrontation, but for very different reasons.
They argue that negotiations with Washington have merely given Iran's adversaries time to regroup and prepare for a stronger attack.
Some have sharply criticized officials who pursued diplomacy and called for Iran to launch a pre-emptive strike if war appears imminent.
“Why shouldn't Iran start the war this time instead of always waiting to be caught off guard?” one user wrote.
Another argued that Iran did not need nuclear weapons to inflict serious damage on its adversaries.
“We don't even need an atomic bomb to retaliate,” the user wrote, arguing instead for strikes on nuclear power plants in Israel and the United Arab Emirates.
The calls for confrontation reflect a very different political outlook from anti-government users hoping outside military action could bring down the Islamic Republic.
But both illustrate how repeated rounds of fighting and failed diplomacy have led some on opposing sides of Iran's political divide to see another war as preferable to the current uncertainty.
Parents prepare for the worst
Parents' concerns about children's safety have intensified following the deaths of more than 100 schoolchildren in a US attack on Minab at the beginning of the recent war.
Some are urging families to keep children home from school if the likelihood of an attack increases. Others are discussing plans to collect children from schools and move them to safer locations as quickly as possible if fighting resumes.
An Instagram post featuring a firefighter has attracted particular attention. The firefighter said that while inspecting safety arrangements at a girls' high school, a school official told them instructions had been issued to prepare identification tags for students.
On Friday, an Education Ministry spokesperson denied that such measures were being implemented and accused “enemies or ignorant individuals” of spreading fear.
One user said they had checked with relatives in Tehran and concluded that the reports were accurate, claiming families they contacted had requested identification tags and were awaiting their delivery.
Fear of another internet blackout
The prospect of another shutdown of international internet access is adding to the anxiety.
Users fear authorities could cut international connectivity immediately if hostilities resume. The prospect is particularly troubling after previous shutdowns made it difficult to contact relatives and access reliable information.
One user recalled that during the war in June last year, the internet was cut several days after fighting began. When war broke out again at the end of February, the shutdown came within hours.
“Now, instead of checking the news in the morning, I open Google's domain to see whether it loads,” the user wrote, “so I can find out whether the war has started.”
Mike Waltz told the Financial Times that Washington still wanted Tehran to return to negotiations and reach what he called a “meaningful agreement” on its nuclear program, but acknowledged the standoff could continue without a deal or a return to prewar shipping levels through the Strait of Hormuz.
“The president and the US Navy can maintain this blockade for the foreseeable future,” Waltz said, adding that the administration was continuing to tighten economic pressure.
He said the US would not consider its objectives achieved until Iran’s highly enriched nuclear material had been dealt with and an agreement reached over domestic uranium enrichment.
Trump considers renewed strikes after midterms
The comments come as Trump is considering several days of renewed strikes against Iran after the midterms, The Atlantic reported, citing officials and people familiar with the discussions.
Potential targets include Iran’s missile and drone arsenal, energy infrastructure and nuclear facilities, according to the report. One outside adviser told the magazine that US economic pressure was working and that additional strikes could push Iran closer to collapse.
An official and another person familiar with the talks said Trump had initially hoped Tehran would return to negotiations before the election, but that had not happened.
US officials stressed that no decision had been made on whether to resume strikes after November 3. The Atlantic said some officials also saw uncertainty over Washington’s next move as a way of keeping Tehran under pressure.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had pushed for another round of strikes before Israel’s election, according to the report, but Trump has so far declined to authorize a new attack before the US vote.
Washington and Tehran trade competing Hormuz messages
The military pressure is unfolding alongside sharply different accounts from Washington and Tehran over control of the Strait of Hormuz.
Trump said on Thursday that more oil had moved through the strait over the previous week than at any point before the war, attributing the increase to the US blockade.
“More oil came out of the Hormuz Strait over the last week than at any time previous, including before the war,” Trump told a campaign rally in Iowa. “That’s because of the blockade.”
He said the blockade had stopped Iran from exporting its own oil and again argued that US military action had destroyed Tehran’s nuclear enrichment capacity.
IRGC says US pushed away from the strait
Iran, however, presented a very different picture on Friday.

articles.title_orig: ‘The worst thing we could do is pick one over the other’: an Australian economist on why US-China competition is ‘a gift’
articles.title_zh: ‘The worst thing we could do is pick one over the other’: an Australian economist on why US-China competition is ‘a gift’
articles.content_orig:
John Edwards reflects on a changing world, economic statecraft and an AI-led manufacturing revival
Get our new political email , free app or daily news podcast
John Edwards wants us to chill out about China.
A former top economic adviser to Paul Keating in the early 1990s, Edwards has been a major figure in the private and public sectors over the past three decades.
Now a non-resident fellow at the Lowy Institute, Edwards has published a new paper titled Overhaul: How Australia can adapt to a changing world economy.
In the paper, Edwards writes that the “vigorous competition and intermittent antagonism” between China, our major economic partner, and the US, our traditional ally and security partner, has long been “mostly a source of anxiety” for Australians.
Yet, Australians should see US-China competition as “a gift”, and we are well placed to become a more prosperous nation over the next 25 years – as long as we play our cards right.
One is that we need to recognise that the US and China will still be the major economies in 25 years. They’re not going to go away. It’s not a race between the two that either can win.
So Australia is in a peculiar position of having a very strong cultural and security relationship with the US, and a very strong economic relationship with China, and we ought to regard that as a great advantage to have such strong links with the two major global economies.
And rather than being anxious about this, we should celebrate it – bearing in mind that the worst possible outcome for Australia is for China and the US to become more adversarial.
It’s better for smaller countries to have two big players than one, and that’s the circumstance in which we find ourselves. So the worst thing we could do is pick one over the other.
So another one is to re-energise our economic statecraft; this is an area where we used to be very good.
In recent years – recent decades – we’ve become dominated by national security considerations, almost to the exclusion of economic statecraft.
[We need] more openness to foreign investment.
On some levels we are. You do see headlines [about how] we’re preparing ourselves for a conflict with China.
I mean, Europe’s not preparing itself for a conflict with China. Canada’s not preparing itself for a conflict with China, and Indonesia’s not, and Malaysia’s not. I’m not sure Japan is, although it says it is. India’s not.
Why would we be preparing for a conflict with China? I think it’s a relatively superficial understanding of our actual position in the world.
Well, I think we do need to be careful to maintain the balance of our relationship with China.
We certainly should not meekly accept China’s sanctions on us, but we should also be very careful not to go out of our way to provoke them.
We have a tiny manufacturing sector. We can almost start from scratch.
We have certain advantages that would become more apparent if we overcome the problem of our labour costs, which are quite high.
[High labour costs] is a good thing – it’s a reflection of the fact that we’ve got high living standards, but they’re an impediment to global manufacturing competitiveness.
And what AI offers us, for the first time in our history, is a way around it. It says we can recommence manufacturing with AI-enabled robots.
But we have to recognise that if we’re going to restore a manufacturing sector in Australia, it’s highly likely to be part of a supply chain that, one way or another, touches on China.
If there’s going to be foreign investment in Australian manufacturing, then it’s highly likely they’ll either be Chinese or influenced by China, and we have to recognise that fact.
No, it’s not a jobs-rich industry, and there’s no way manufacturing is going to be jobs-rich in the future.
There is a lot of short-termism in our comprehension of what’s happening in the global economy, and it’s useful every now and then to step back and say, ‘Well, actually, what has been going on?’
And as I say, if you look at the last 25 years, calamitous though they were in many respects, the economic outcomes were pretty good and replicated those of the previous 50 years.
I think there are several things going on. In the case of the US, it’s the awareness that China now matches it in economic weight.
The other thing in the US is just unchecked growth of inequality, and particularly the outstanding growth in the wealth, power and prestige of the top 1% of the population. It’s unprecedented.
In Europe, it’s slow growth in living standards compared to a lot of other places, including Australia. A discordant migration story.
But a generally gloomy view is not true of India, and not true of China or of many other countries which have done extremely well.
I just can’t account for it, because we’ve done well.
We’ve got problems now. We’ve got high inflation, which we need to restrain. And we’ve got very low growth in productivity – it’ll be a very good thing when that revives.
But in terms of our long-term outlook, it’s pretty good.
I guess it is. But it’s basically a supply-side issue which we’re beginning, I think, to address.

A total of 100 people were arrested in Barcelona on Saturday evening after hooded demonstrators who participated in an anti-establishment rally looted shops and set fire to street furniture around the city's central Plaza de Catalunya.
Núria Parlon, the interior minister for the Spanish region of Catalonia , said around 25% of those arrested were minors. More than 30 fires were set and 14 stores vandalized or looted in a part of town popular with tourists and weekend shoppers, she added.
Demonstrators were called in social media posts to a movement "against the system." The posts also used the slogan "Institut Indignats," a translation of the movement "Lyceés Indignés," which was used to rally students who have protested in France in recent weeks. In English, the phrase translates as "Indignant High School Student."
Social media videos show people trapped inside shops, including department store El Corte Inglés, after shutters were lowered to prevent looting . Other posts showed hooded demonstrators dressed in black kicking in shop windows and making off with goods, in some cases encouraged by online viewers.
Barcelona Mayor Jaume Collboni said acts of vandalism in the city "will not go unpunished," including legal consequences for the guardians of any minors involved.
